body.objective: Students will be able to practise winter travel and safety skills.
body.iCan: I can practise winter travel and safety skills.
successCriteria: I can travel safely on snowshoes

body.hook: Long before snowmobiles and Gore-Tex, people travelled across this land all winter. Snowshoes were developed by Indigenous peoples of North America and are still one of the best ways to move through deep snow. Winter isn't a season to hide from; with the right skills, it's a season to explore.

study.title: Winter Trek
study.question: How do people travel safely and enjoyably in winter?
study.passage:
Part 1, Snowshoe skills (15 minutes): Put on snowshoes with a partner check (bindings snug, toes centred). Practise:
• Walking with a slightly wider stance so frames don't hit
• Kick-stepping uphill and leaning back slightly downhill
• Turning in a wide arc
• Using poles for balance
Part 2, Winter hazards (10 minutes):
• Cold: use layers and buddy checks every 20 minutes (cheeks, nose, ears, fingers).
• Darkness: in an Alberta winter, it can be dark by around 5:00 p.m. Set a turnaround time.
• Ice: never walk on lakes or rivers unless the ice has been measured and confirmed safe. The Canadian Red Cross recommends at least 15 cm of clear, solid ice for walking alone. River ice and snow-covered ice are especially unreliable.
• Snow and wind: stay on marked trails; know avalanche terrain is a separate hazard needing special training.
Part 3, Group trek (25 minutes): Groups of five snowshoe a marked course. One student is the trip leader, one the "sweep" (always last), and one the time-keeper who calls the turnaround time. Do two buddy checks on the way.
Part 4, Debrief: What went well? What would you change on a real outing?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; ice-safety guidance from the Canadian Red Cross.

body.objective: Students will be able to plan an outdoor activity for peers.

body.hook: Leading an outdoor activity is very different from joining one. Before anyone steps outside, a good leader has already pictured what could go wrong, planned for it and set clear expectations.

study.title: Plan to Lead
study.question: How do I plan a safe, engaging outdoor activity for my peers?
study.passage:
Leading task (written for this lesson): in pairs or threes, plan a 20-minute outdoor activity for classmates on the school grounds or a nearby park, e.g. a snowshoe or walking route with nature stops, a winter shelter-building challenge, a tracking hunt, a compass course, or a cooperative game.
Activity plan: goal (what should participants learn or experience?); location and boundaries; timing (arrive, brief, activity, debrief); equipment; roles of each leader.
Risk assessment table: hazard → likelihood (low/medium/high) → severity (minor/moderate/serious) → controls. Example: icy path (medium, moderate) → choose a route away from ice, walk not run, check footwear. Cold (medium, moderate) → check clothing at the briefing, keep moving, set a 20-minute limit, warm-up spot indoors. Lost participant (low, serious) → clear boundaries, buddy system, head counts at start and end, whistle signal.
Briefing script (2 minutes): welcome, goal, boundaries, buddy system, signals (whistle = gather), safety rules, what to do if hurt, questions.
Teacher approves each plan before it runs.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to lead and debrief the activity.

body.hook: Leadership day. You've planned it; now you run it. Afterwards, a debrief helps everyone understand what they learned, and helps you grow as a leader.

study.title: Lead and Debrief
study.question: How do I lead an activity and help the group learn from it?
study.passage:
Leading checklist (written for this lesson):
Before: check equipment and route; confirm boundaries; check participants' clothing.
During: give your briefing; count heads; position leaders (one at the front, one at the back, "sweep"); watch for cold, fatigue or anyone left out; adapt if needed (shorten the route, add a warm-up game, move to shelter).
Debrief (5 minutes), using What? So what? Now what?: What happened? (describe). So what? (what did we learn, how did it feel?). Now what? (how will we use it?). Ask open questions, let everyone speak, keep it positive and honest.
Feedback: participants complete a quick card: one thing the leaders did well, one suggestion. Teacher observes using a leadership rubric: safety, communication, group management, inclusion, adaptability.
Leader reflection: what went as planned, what you adapted and why, how you would lead differently next time.
